title: Code analysis
summary: Reasoning about code without running it: counting steps, keeping behaviour through refactors, reading dense code and spotting hidden side effects.

concepts.title: Time and space complexity of real code
Pure functions and hidden side effects

misconceptions.description: Believes break inside an inner loop is ignored when counting, so every inner pass still runs.
Believes a nested loop visits each pair only once, ignoring that the inner loop restarts every time.
Believes a Set lookup scans every earlier value like includes on an array.
Believes the work of a loop depends on how many results it produces rather than how much input it reads.
Believes code written for the parent class always runs the parent's setter, even on a subclass object.
Believes overriding a setter in a subclass also changes the parent class for its own objects.
Believes overwriting a key while spreading either moves it to the end or leaves its old value.
Believes adding one more branch to an if chain keeps code closed for modification.
Believes sort returns a sorted copy and leaves the original array in its old order.
Believes sort has no visible effect unless its result is assigned to a variable.
Believes reading a key that is missing from an object throws an error instead of giving undefined.
Believes 0 and undefined are interchangeable because both are falsy, so a truthiness test equals a test for undefined.
Believes filter removes items from the array it is called on.
Believes an array passed to a function is copied, so the function cannot change the caller's array.

lessons.title: Time and space complexity of real code

conceptCard.title: Counting steps
conceptCard.body: To judge cost, count how many times the busiest line runs. One loop over n items runs it n times. A loop inside a loop runs it n times n. Early exits and direct lookups can do less work than a scan.

conceptCard.title: Same inputs, same outputs
conceptCard.body: Refactoring changes the shape of code, not what it does. After a change, the same inputs must give the same outputs, including edge cases such as 0 and undefined. Moving code into a subclass or a new class is a refactor too: compare the old and new versions on the same inputs.

conceptCard.title: Reading from the inside out
conceptCard.body: Dense code is easier to read in small parts. Find what each function returns, then what each argument is on the first call. Evaluate the innermost call first and work outward. A factory returns a function that remembers its outer variables; a lookup table replaces a chain of ifs.

lessons.title: Pure functions and hidden side effects

conceptCard.title: Pure and impure functions
conceptCard.body: A pure function returns a value that depends only on its arguments and changes nothing else. Pushing to a list, sorting in place or assigning to a parameter's property are hidden side effects: the caller's data changes too.

items.prompt: A library clerk hunts for two books whose page counts add up to 20. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The inner loop ends early only for the 16, and the counter keeps every pass made before each break.
You counted four full passes of four. The break ends the inner loop early for one book, so fewer checks run.
That total fits a loop that visits each pair once. This inner loop starts from the first book every time.

items.explanation: break ends only the inner loop. The first three books each scan all four items; the last book matches on its first pass. That is 4 + 4 + 4 + 1 checks.
hints: Look at what break stops: the inner loop or the outer one.
Count the inner passes separately for each book in the outer loop.
Does the inner loop finish all four passes for every book?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The loop lists repeated ids. Which statement about how its work grows with the number of ids is true?

options.text: Each id costs a fixed amount of work, so doubling the ids roughly doubles the work.
options.feedback: Right. One pass, and each has and add takes roughly the same time however many ids came before.

options.text: has() looks at every earlier id, so doubling the ids roughly quadruples the work.
options.feedback: That describes searching an array with includes. A Set jumps straight to the value instead of scanning.

options.text: The work depends on the duplicates found, so a list with none costs almost nothing.
options.feedback: Every id is still read and added, duplicates or not. The size of the output does not set the cost of the loop.

items.explanation: Set lookups and inserts take roughly constant time, so each id costs a fixed amount of work and the total grows in step with the list. Cost follows the input read, not the output.
hints: Think about what one has call has to do.
A Set finds a value by its hash, not by walking through the earlier values.
Compare the work per id when the list has 5 ids and when it has 500.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The average should be worked out once, so steps should print 5, but it prints 25. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The first pass fills sum, and every later pass reuses it, so the list is summed only once.
sum starts at 0, so this test is never true: nothing is ever summed and the comparison no longer uses the real total.
The list is still summed on every pass, and the running total keeps growing, so the comparison is wrong as well.

items.explanation: total(ids) walks the whole list, and calling it inside the loop repeats that walk for every item, so the work grows with the list length squared. Filling sum on the first pass only keeps the result the same and walks the list once.
hints: Compare the steps printed with the length of the list: which work happens again on every pass?
The value total(ids) returns is the same on every pass, so it only needs to be computed once.
sum is declared before the loop and starts at 0; decide when the loop should fill it.

items.prompt: Before a refactor the list held two Box objects and the loop printed [20, 20]. The refactor swapped the second one for a Bin. What does the program print now?

options.feedback: Right. The Bin runs its own setter, so the refactor changed the output.
You ran the parent setter for both, as before the refactor. A subclass setter takes over for its own objects.
The override belongs to Bin only. Box objects still run the setter written in Box.

items.explanation: A setter in a subclass replaces the parent's setter for that subclass only. The Box stores 20, but the Bin caps it at 9, so the swap is not a safe refactor: the output changed.
hints: Look at which class each object in the array comes from.
A subclass setter overrides the parent's only for its own objects.
Apply each object's own setter to 20, in array order.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: ok replaces old in a tidy-up meant to keep behaviour. Which statement explains why the two numbers differ?

options.text: The tests disagree on the value 0, so the tidy-up changed behaviour for that input.
options.feedback: Right. old drops 0 as falsy, ok keeps it, so the same input gives different results.

options.text: Both tests reject 0 and undefined alike, so old and ok are equivalent.
options.feedback: Only undefined is rejected by ok. 0 is falsy but is not undefined, so it passes that test.

options.text: filter removes items from ps, so the second call sees a shorter list.
options.feedback: filter builds a new array and leaves ps unchanged, so both calls see the same three values.

items.explanation: A refactor must give the same output for every input, including 0 and undefined. old keeps only truthy values, so 0 is dropped and it counts 2. ok rejects only undefined, so it counts 3. The two are not equivalent.
hints: Run both tests by hand on each value of ps, one at a time.
A refactor must give the same output for the same input, edge cases included.
Compare what each test does with the value 0.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Before a refactor this printed [3, 0]: every log with a km value counts. Now it drops one log. Tap the line that changed the behaviour and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. in asks whether the property exists, so a km of 0 stays and the empty log leaves.
A km of 0 is still dropped, so the behaviour stays different from the original.
This keeps the empty log and drops the zero, which prints the opposite mix of logs.

items.explanation: A truthiness test drops a km of 0 as well as a missing km. The original rule was about presence, so the test must ask whether the property exists.
hints: Run the filter on the log whose km is 0.
Truthiness and presence are different questions.
Pick the test that asks only whether km exists.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The old tip function used 10 when no percent was given and kept 0 as 0. Fill the blank so the refactor prints 5 0 10.

options.feedback: Right. Only an absent percent falls back to 10.
An absent pct is not 0, so it stays undefined and the first tip is NaN.
A percent of 0 is falsy, so it becomes 10 and the second tip is wrong.
This gives 10 only when pct is truthy and gives undefined when absent, so the output is wrong.
This ignores the argument, so 0 and 20 both become 10.

items.explanation: ?? falls back only for null or undefined, so an explicit 0 stays 0. || treats 0 as missing and would replace it.
hints: Check what each chip does when pct is 0.
Only an absent value should get the default.
Only one chip gives 10 for an absent percent and still keeps an explicit 0.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A garden shop labels its plant tags with a dense reducer. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The second b updates its value but the key keeps its first position.
Keys keep their first position when overwritten. The second b does not move to the end.
The later write wins: the second b replaces the 0 with its index.

items.explanation: The spread copies b first, then [t]: i overwrites its value but keeps its place. The object ends with b at index 2 and a at index 1, with b still listed first.
hints: Work out what the reducer holds after each tag.
Overwriting an existing key keeps the key's original position.
Follow b twice: where does it sit after the second time?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Read the program from the inside out. Which statement explains why pie adds nothing, and how a new kind would get a price?

options.text: priceOf looks the key up in cost and falls back to 0, so pie adds 0. Pricing pie means adding a key to cost.
options.feedback: Right. The data lives in the table, and bill and priceOf stay as they are.

options.text: bill has one branch per kind, so pie needs a new branch inside bill.
options.feedback: bill has no branches. It maps each key through priceOf, which reads the table.

options.text: The program throws for pie, because cost has no pie key.
options.feedback: Reading a missing key does not throw. It gives undefined, which the ?? operator replaces.

items.explanation: Work from the inside out: cost[k] gives a price or undefined, ?? 0 turns a missing one into 0, map prices every key and reduce adds them. Pie is missing, so it adds 0; adding pie to cost would price it.
hints: Start with line 2: what does priceOf return for a key that is not in cost?
Evaluate the innermost call first: priceOf, then map, then reduce.
Where would the price of pie be written so that no function changes?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Two door counters should count separately and print 3 1, but the program prints 3 4. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. Each call of mk creates its own n, so b counts on its own.
This stores the factory itself, so a() builds a counter instead of counting.
A different step still calls mk only once, so both names share one counter.

items.explanation: Evaluated from the inside out, mk(1) runs once and fill copies that one function into both slots, so both names share one closure. Each counter needs its own call of the factory.
hints: Evaluate line 5 from the inside out: how many times is mk called?
A closure keeps the variables of the call that created it, and fill copies one value into every slot.
Each counter needs a call of its own.

items.prompt: Read the dense function f. Write the body of newRecords(scores) so it returns exactly what f returns for the same list.
items.explanation: f keeps a score only when it beats both zero and every score kept so far. A first 0 does not count, and a tie does not count. A running top starting at 0 does the same.
hints: Work out f on a list that starts with 0.
f compares each score with the largest score kept, never below 0.
Keep a top that starts at 0 and update it when a score is above it.

items.prompt: A canteen helper finds the cheapest price on a list. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. sort reordered menu itself, so its first item is now the cheapest one.
sort does not make a copy. It reorders the original array too.
The sort really runs on the array, so the cheapest comes first in both reads.

items.explanation: sort reorders the array it is called on and returns that same array. The helper reads the first item and also leaves the caller's list sorted, which is a hidden side effect.
hints: Ask whether sort works on a copy or on the array itself.
Methods that sort in place change the caller's data.
Print the second value after the helper has run, not before.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: sum should only read orders, yet the second line printed is not the original order. Which statement explains it?

options.text: sum sorts the array it receives in place, a hidden side effect that changes the data of its caller.
options.feedback: Right. list is the same array as orders, so sorting it changes what the caller sees.

options.text: sort returns a sorted copy, so orders is replaced by that copy.
options.feedback: sort changes the array it runs on and returns that same array. Nothing is copied or replaced.

options.text: Passing an array to a function copies it, so orders only changes if sum returns the list.
options.feedback: The parameter refers to the same array, not a copy, so changes made inside are visible outside.

items.explanation: list and orders are the same array, and sort reorders an array in place. That is a hidden side effect: the caller sees different data after the call. A pure sum would sort a copy or just add the two numbers.
hints: Compare the array printed on the last line with the one on line 1.
A pure function changes nothing outside itself, and an argument that is an array is shared with the caller.
Which line inside sum changes the array it was given?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: withSize should return a resized copy and leave base alone, so the program prints M XL. Tap the line that changes base and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The target is a new object, so base stays untouched.
The first argument is still s, so base still changes.

items.explanation: Object.assign writes into its first argument. Passing the original object changes it. Passing a new empty object first builds a copy and keeps the later values.
hints: Which object is the first argument of Object.assign?
Object.assign changes its first argument and returns it.
Start from a new empty object, then add the old values, then the new size.
